extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary travel essays / general 19th-century literate audience
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive, reflective travel letters/essays that record journeys, landscapes, local history, and social observation, often addressed to a general readership and illustrated with literary allusions and anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid sensory landscape description
rubrics_metrics.description: Give detailed, sensory accounts of scenes so the reader can 'look' with the writer (e.g., Dungeon-Ghyll Force: winding path, sound of falling water, narrow fissure of sky; Loch Katrine and Ben Lomond descriptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete images and sensory detail (sound, sight, atmosphere) and frame moments so they evoke emotional and intellectual responses (e.g., 'you see the sky through a fissure so narrow as to make it look very pure and distant'). Allow scenes to 'bide their time' in the mind before attempting full description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary allusion to enrich place
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect places to poems, poets, and literature (references to Wordsworth's 'Excursion', Scott's 'Lady of the Lake', Burns, Ossianic associations) to deepen meaning and resonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke canonical works and poets whose tone or themes match the landscape; quote or paraphrase relevant passages to let literary memory illuminate the scene ('I recognized the tone and atmosphere of that noble poem').

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal narrative and travel logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Report modes of travel, companions, timings, and the practicalities of the journey (coach vs. railroad, time spent, how travel is accomplished).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete travel details to set context and to reflect on how the mode of travel shapes experience (e.g., preference for coach travel as enabling observation vs. railroad as 'the most stupid process on earth').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anecdote and dialogue to characterize people
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell short stories and report speech (e.g., Burns' banquet anecdote, conversations with publishers, boatmen singing Gaelic songs) to present personalities and local color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose well-observed anecdotes that reveal character and moral quality; include reported speech and small scenes to animate the narrative ('He drank off the wine, and thundered forth...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and social commentary embedded in description
rubrics_metrics.description: Use travel observations as a springboard for ethical or social critique (inequalities near country houses, publishers' treatment of authors, Corn Laws, poverty in cities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not separate beauty from social reality; contrast picturesque scenes with nearby misery and offer candid reflection or advocacy ('it is impossible to forget the frightful inequalities between the lot of man and man').

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate historical associations and local lore
rubrics_metrics.description: Weave in historical anecdotes, local stories, and legendary figures (Queen Mary at Loch Leven, Rob Roy, Johnnie Armstrong, Branxholm Goblin Page) to situate the visit in time and tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring forward castles, ballads, and reputed local memories to give places depth and human continuity; note how oral tradition shapes locals' claims about events ('They replied, "Certainly; it had been told from father to son"').

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation and poetry to amplify themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use extended quotations of verse or poetry (e.g., full Burns song 'For a' that') to epitomize a theme or moral impression drawn from the journey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select poems that resonate thematically and present them in full or in part to let the verse speak as an interpretive lens for the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest critical appraisal of monuments and art
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess cultural artifacts and public monuments candidly (criticizing Scott's monument posture, Burns statue unworthiness), not merely praising them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer measured critical judgments that balance reverence for genius with aesthetic honesty ('The statue is too much hid within the monument... wants that majesty of repose').

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective personal voice and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a personal, reflective first-person tone that admits lapses and deliberation ('I have too long delayed writing up my journal'; 'the mind does not now furnish congenial colors').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the writer's temperament show through; use self-reflection about timing, memory, and mood to frame the narrative and guide selection of material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt recording of observations to avoid loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Write up impressions before they fade: 'Many interesting observations slip from recollection if one waits so many days.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record details soon after seeing them to preserve freshness; delay risks losing useful particulars and tonal nuance.
